questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Firstly, the language. I have always wanted to improve my German, and learning a language is a completely different challenge to studying a Master's degree in Law (in your own language).  

Secondly, the city. It seemed like the perfect opportunity to study German law in one of the most vibrant and diverse cities in Europe. I had visited Berlin a few times before my exchange but I wanted to be able to really get to know the city and make use of all the opportunities it has to offer. Especially the food scene and cultural experiences. 

Thirdly, the international recognition of Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and the courses offered by it.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had high expectations before I arrived in Berlin, but I never imagined that I would be so fortunate to experience so much and meet so many new people. I truly fell in love with the city and I plan on visiting Berlin many times in the future. I strongly recommend to go on an exchange to Berlin - you will not regret it!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
It was fairly easy once I took the time to research properly, but the Humboldt-website (Agnes) can be quite confusing in the beginning and a good German proficiency level helps a lot. But Humboldt sent all of the Information that I needed a few months prior to the beginning of the semester. 

The only thing that wasn't easy to find out was the expected exam dates. The law faculty at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin has a very different system when it comes to registering for exams. The exam dates needs to be cleared with each professor, so you need to write to them individually. And the exams in the courses recommended for Erasmus students at the Law Faculty are usually held before the stated exam period for the rest of the law students. During my exchange I eventually found out when I could expect the exams to be held but it was quite frustrating not knowing when the semester actually ended in order to e.g. apply for the Erasmus Grant and plan ahead in general.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Humboldt offers a "studis4studis" programme, where you get a mentor.

However, I didn't register for the programme and the written information sent by Humboldt prior to the beginning of the semester and a "Zoom-Info-Meeting" was overall sufficient. Humboldt also helped with information regarding how to book an appointment at the Bürgeramt for the "Abmeldung" (a form you need to fill out in order to register your address in Berlin).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found quite affordable housing at Airbnb in Kreuzberg, but I booked it 1,5 year in advance, so this is probably only an option if you have started searching for housing early.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is amazing to live in districts like Kreuzberg, Neukölln and Friedrichshain - this is where everything happens. I believe that Humboldt offers housing quite far away from the university and everything else, so if you have the opportunity to find housing elsewhere, I strongly recommend that you do. It is such a cool opportunity to really get to know the city.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You can find all of the available courses at
agnes.hu-berlin.de
under Vorlesungsverzeichnis/Course Catalog.
The first two weeks of the semester you have the opportunity to visit all of the courses you are interested in before making your final decision.
During these two weeks you need to ask the professors for the "Einschreibeschlüssel" needed for each course in order to access them at Moodle (the intranet at Humboldt), where all of the material and powerpints etc. will be uploaded.
You also have to ask the professors individually if they offer exams for Erasmus students. I strongly recommend that you specifically ask what kind of format the exam has.
However, most of the professors will not tell you, when the exam can be expected to be held, so don't bother asking at all until halfway into the semester. I believe it's simply because they can't tell yet, when they have the time to conduct the exams. They will, however, probably let you know about a month or so in advance.
At the end of these two weeks you need to fill out an online form, which is sent to you in an e-mail by the administration. Here you make your final decision on which exams you want to take.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Only an overall explanation on how to register, but you need to contact the professors yourself.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Visit as many lectures as you can - especially in order to: 

1. get an idea of the required prior knowledge about German law and
2. see if you can actually understand (most of) what the professor says during the lecture. Some of them speaks very clearly - and some of them don't. This was crucial for me since I took all of my courses in German.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was high enough, but the most of the courses are only 5 ECTS - so definitely manageable.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Very different. The courses where mostly taught with lectures where the professors doesn't involve the students that much, but it depends on the professor. Two of my courses had quite a lot of cases and discussions in plenum. The curriculum is mainly what is said during the lecture and the professors only recommend certain literature (that usually isn't recommended to Erasmus students). I bought one recommended book and that was probably a waste of money.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Privates Baurecht und Vertragsgestaltung (5 ECTS)
- NS-Unrecht (5 ECTS)
- Internationales Privatrecht (5 ECTS)
- Legal Tech - Einführung in rechtliche, technische und wirtschaftlich-organisatorische Grundlagen (5 ECTS)
- IT für Juristen (5 ECTS)
- Einführung ind das internationale und europäische Steuerrecht (5 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I can especially recommend the following courses: 

1. Privates Baurecht and Vertragsgestaltung. The professor is so nice to Erasmus students and gives a lot of examples during the lecture. This makes it way easier to stay focused, which can be quite hard when German is your second foreign language. 

2. NS-Unrecht. Even though this course, during the semester, seemed extremely hard and almost impossible to pass, it was definitely manageable. The professor was so nice and the exam was very surprisingly a really good experience. The topic is so interesting and a unique opportunity to learn something about German history and how the Nazi-regime has influenced German law. But it is by far the course I had to study the most for. Less could probably have been sufficient. 

3. IT für Juristen. The professor was so cool and it was so much fun to try and learn to code (which was an optional part of the lecture). The lecture itself involved cases and discussions in plenum, and there were quite a few online lectures, that we had to watch prior to each lecture. This was, however, also manageable.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not expect to spend so much money on food - but it was almost impossible for me to resist the temptation to try out as many as possible of the amazing restaurants that Berlin has to offer. Both the cheaper options and the more fancy ones (which btw still are way cheaper compared to restaurants offering similar standards in Copenhagen).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Insurance was cheaper than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Humboldt offers a lot of sport activities (HU Hochschulsport). But make sure to register in time - a lot of them are sold out quickly.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Try out a new sport through HU Hochschulsport - I tried out top rope climbing and it was so cool to meet other people through a sport activity.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I never went outside of Berlin. The city has enough to offer.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy - but it is really hard to adjust to the language in the beginning. But it got quickly easier and my German improved greatly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be social - you have to take initiative yourself.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Having to pay in cash all the time and having to speak and write in a formal tone to the professors.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The diversity and the food scene in Berlin. But mostly the culture to go out and use the city instead of only hosting private events or staying home. Berlin is so much more vibrant than Copenhagen and it is evident, that locals really spend most of their free time in public spaces and parks. This creates an amazing atmosphere.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't be afraid of taking courses in German! 

2. Take the intensive German course offered by Humboldt! The teachers are so good and I met most of the people I ended up hanging out with throughout the whole semester at my language course.  

3. Apply for scholarships early. And apply for a lot of them.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Berlin is fantastic during summer - so choose to go there during the summer semester!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting so many new people from all over the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The language - but it is so rewarding to see how quickly you improve if you make an effort.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
